title: At the Core of Student Apathy…
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that behind student apathy lies pain rather than indifference. He recasts the five key beliefs behind student motivation as five key fears: anti-credibility, anti-value, anti-belonging, anti-effort, and anti-efficacy, each written in the voice of a student who wishes things were otherwise. The central insight is that humans are made for engagement and progress, so an apathetic student is a hurting student, not a lazy one. He asks teachers to hold that empathy through the day and to resolve again to do the work that matters most. He ends on the hopeful claim that these beliefs are malleable and can be shifted one unit, lesson, and interaction at a time.
points: Apathy is better understood as a symptom of pain than as a character flaw.
Each of the five motivation beliefs has a shadow fear that can be heard in an apathetic student's inner voice.
No student dreams of becoming unmotivated, so empathy is the right starting posture for teachers.
Because the beliefs are malleable, teachers can shift them through small, repeated actions in units, lessons, and interactions.
quotes: When we see motivated students, what we’re seeing are human beings benefitting from the five key beliefs. On the flipside, when we see unmotivated or apathetic students, we’re seeing the dark sides of these five key beliefs. Think of them as the five key fears.

Anti-Credibility: I want my teacher to be good at his job, but he’s not. He doesn’t care about me, or he doesn’t know how to teach me, or he has no sense of urgency about this lesson, this unit, this year of my life.
Anti-Value: I wish the things I have to do in school — reading, writing, discussion, knowledge-building — mattered too my life, but it doesn’t. I wish it wasn’t boring, but it is — and boring is bad.
Anti-Effort: I wish that the work of learning she’s teaching me to put forth was going to pay off if I really try at it, but I don’t think it will. When it comes to math, I’m stuck.

These thoughts stir in the hearts of our apathetic students. And perhaps the most fundamental insight to have in these situations is that apathy is a kind of pain. Human beings are not designed for apathy — they are designed for engagement, for progress, for development, for learning.

Tomorrow, consider that: no human wants to be unmotivated and apathetic. Your students don’t want to feel that the work is pointless, or that they’re doomed to fail, or that they don’t belong. Reflect on it throughout the day.
